title: Matching and Simplifying Charts for an Audience
summary: Learn to match chart type to the specific stakeholder point (bar for comparison, line for trend, pie for part-to-whole, boxplot with caution), then simplify the chosen chart by removing gridlines, borders, trailing zeros, rotated labels, and unnecessary data labels.

steps.title: The chart you pick should match the point you are making
steps.lede: The same delivery data can be shown as a bar chart, a pie chart, or a line plot — but only one will make your specific point land for the operations manager.

blocks.text: During your own exploration you might have built several charts of SwiftMove Nigeria's delivery data. Presenting to the operations manager, the question changes: which chart actually makes the point you need to make, for this audience? Chart choice is driven by the point, not by the data alone.

A bar chart is used for graphing categorical data and comparing values across categories — showing average delivery time side by side for Lagos, Abuja, and Kano. A line graph is best when you want to show how a value changes over time — for example, Lagos delivery time rising week over week. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing distributions side by side, but they may be unfamiliar to many audiences and could introduce a learning curve; a bar chart or line plot can often make the same point more directly.

steps.title: Why the chart type must match the point you are making

blocks.group_title: Why the chart type must match the point you are making

segments.label: Bar chart vs. pie chart: comparing values across categories
segments.summary: The same time-use data (sleep, work, eat, rest) is shown first as a pie chart, then as a bar chart. The pie makes it hard to judge which slice is larger when two slices are close in size. The bar chart, with its common baseline, makes the one-hour difference between working and sleeping immediately readable. A second example pits two pie charts against a grouped bar chart to answer 'does Earl work more than Herman, and by how much?' — a question the pies struggle to answer and the bar chart resolves at a glance.

segments.label: Boxplots: strong for distributions, but risky with unfamiliar audiences
segments.summary: A boxplot is considered as a candidate for showing distributions across multiple groups. Two practical problems emerge: sparse data on some days would produce boxes with no box body, and — more broadly — boxplots are not a widely recognised chart type, so an audience unfamiliar with them faces a steeper learning curve. The presenter notes that a specialist audience (researchers and physicians) may be the exception, but still sets the boxplot aside in favour of continuing to explore other options.

bridge.before: Watch how the same data looks different depending on chart type, and notice when a chart makes comparison easy versus hard. The first clip argues strongly for bars over pies; Devspace's text also covers when a pie is the right choice.
bridge.after: The first clip demonstrates f1 and counters the pie-slice comparison misconception; the second covers f3 and f5. Neither clip addresses part-to-whole framing (f4) or scatterplots (f6) — the text covers both.

steps.title: Pie charts, scatterplots, and a comparison trap
steps.lede: Part-to-whole framing calls for a pie chart — but comparing pie slices is harder than it looks.

blocks.text: A pie chart expresses a part-to-whole relationship in the data. It is best used for a general sense of how parts relate to the whole, or to highlight that one segment is notably larger or smaller than the others — and the pie must depict a meaningful whole (values that sum to 100%). If the point is 'Lagos accounts for most of our total delivery volume,' a pie chart of city order shares fits that framing in a way a bar chart of averages would not.

A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience. It is not the default choice for a non-technical stakeholder presentation, but if the distance-versus-delivery-time relationship needs to go in front of the operations manager, a scatterplot can work.

It can look like comparing pie slices is just as easy as comparing bar lengths — but it is not. A bar chart's aligned, common baseline makes length differences easy to judge; two pie slices of similar size are harder to rank correctly by eye. When precise comparison between categories matters, a bar chart is the stronger choice.

steps.title: Scatterplot: exploratory or communicative?
steps.lede: A scatterplot of delivery distance versus delivery time sits on your screen. Is it ready for the operations manager, or is it still an exploratory tool?

public.prompt: You have built a scatterplot showing delivery distance vs. delivery time for all orders. The operations manager asks to see it in the presentation. What should you consider before including it?

options.text: Scatterplots are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it; consider whether a simpler chart type would make the point more directly for this audience.
Scatterplots are the best choice for showing relationships between two variables, so include it without changes.
Scatterplots are too technical for any stakeholder presentation and should never be used.
The scatterplot is fine as long as you add gridlines to help the manager read exact values.

opt_b.message: Not quite. While scatterplots are useful for exploring relationships, they are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. For a non-technical audience, a simpler chart type may make the point more directly.

opt_c.message: Not quite. Scatterplots can be designed to convey findings to an audience, though they are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. The key is to consider whether a simpler chart type would make the point more directly for this specific audience.

opt_d.message: Not quite. Adding gridlines doesn't address the core issue: scatterplots are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. For a non-technical stakeholder, consider whether a simpler chart type would make the point more directly.

correct.message: Correct. A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it, though it can still be designed to convey findings to an audience. For a non-technical stakeholder, consider whether a simpler chart type would make the point more directly.

incorrect.message: Review the glossary's guidance on when scatterplots are typically used and consider the audience's familiarity with different chart types.

steps.title: Remove the clutter your audience doesn't need
steps.lede: A chart built for your own exploration can carry gridlines, a border, and precise decimal labels. The operations manager probably doesn't need any of that to get the point.

blocks.text: A bar chart of city delivery times built during your own exploration can carry gridlines, a border, and precise decimal labels that help you double-check the numbers. The operations manager probably doesn't need any of that to get the point. Each element you remove reduces the visual effort required to read the chart.

Gridlines can be deleted from a chart; if precise values matter to the audience, label the data point directly instead of relying on gridlines. A chart's border can be removed, since it is not adding informative value — white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border.

Data labels should be used sparingly, only where exact values are important; otherwise remove them and use the axis instead. Unnecessary trailing zeroes can be dropped — '22.00' becomes '22 min'. Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read; city names like Lagos, Abuja, and Kano are short enough to render horizontally.

steps.title: Decluttering a chart for a non-technical audience

blocks.group_title: Decluttering a chart for a non-technical audience

segments.label: Removing chart clutter: border, gridlines, trailing zeros, diagonal labels, and excess data labels
segments.summary: The presenter opens by explaining that every chart element adds cognitive burden, and that overwhelming an audience risks losing them entirely — establishing why decluttering matters. Working on a bar chart in Excel, they remove the chart border (noting white space does the job of separation better), delete the gridlines and shaded background, then reformat the y-axis to drop trailing zeros by switching to thousands units with a 'k' suffix. They then abbreviate the diagonal month labels on the x-axis to horizontal text, citing research that diagonal text takes fifty percent longer to read. Finally, they weigh whether exact values are needed: deciding they are not, they delete all data labels and keep the y-axis instead, leaving a much cleaner chart.

bridge.before: Watch how each removal reduces reading effort. Note: the presenter uses Excel; the same design principles apply in any charting tool. The clip does not demonstrate labelling a data point directly when precision matters (f1).
bridge.after: The clip shows f2–f6 applied in sequence. Devspace's text also covers f1: when precise values are essential, label the data point directly rather than restoring gridlines.

blocks.text: Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph.

steps.title: Which elements should you remove to reduce chart clutter?
steps.lede: The operations manager will see this bar chart in a slide deck. Identify which elements add visual effort without adding information.

public.prompt: A bar chart of city delivery times has a visible border, gridlines, trailing-zero axis labels (e.g. '22.00 minutes'), rotated city-name tick labels, and data labels on every bar. Which elements should you remove to reduce chart clutter for the operations manager?

options.text: Remove the border, gridlines, trailing zeros, rotated labels, and per-bar data labels — all add visual effort without adding information.
Keep the gridlines and border to help the manager read exact values; remove only the data labels.
Remove only the border and gridlines; keep the trailing zeros and rotated labels for precision.
Remove the gridlines but keep the border to separate the chart from the slide background.

opt_b.message: Not quite. Gridlines can be deleted; if precise values matter, label the data point directly instead. A chart border is not adding informative value — white space separates parts of a visual better than a border. Trailing zeros and rotated labels also add visual effort without adding information.

opt_c.message: Not quite. Trailing zeros can be dropped from axis labels (e.g. '22.00' becomes '22 min'), and diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read — labels can be abbreviated so they render horizontally instead. Both add visual effort without adding information.

opt_d.message: Not quite. A chart border is not adding informative value — white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border. Removing the border reduces one more element the audience must look past to reach the data.

correct.message: Correct. All five elements — border, gridlines, trailing zeros, rotated labels, and per-bar data labels — add visual effort without adding information. Removing them reduces clutter and lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph.

incorrect.message: Review which chart elements add visual effort without adding information, and consider the role of white space in separating visual elements.

hints: Consider which elements add visual effort without adding information.
Think about what the glossary says about gridlines, borders, trailing zeros, rotated labels, and data labels.

public.prompt: A colleague says the chart border helps separate the chart from the slide background. What is the better alternative, and why?

options.text: White space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border; the border is not adding informative value, just one more element the eye must process.
The border is essential for separation; without it, the chart would blend into the slide.
Add a thicker border and a shadow effect to make the separation even clearer.
Keep the border but make it a lighter color so it is less distracting.

opt_b.message: Not quite. A chart border is not adding informative value. White space around the chart already differentiates it from the surrounding content, and does so better than a border. Removing the border reduces one more element the audience must look past to reach the data.

opt_c.message: Not quite. Adding more visual elements (thicker border, shadow) increases clutter rather than reducing it. White space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border, and the border is not adding informative value.

opt_d.message: Not quite. Even a lighter border is still an element the eye must process. A chart border is not adding informative value — white space can differentiate parts of a visual better than a border. Removing the border entirely reduces one more element the audience must look past to reach the data.

correct.message: Correct. A chart border is not adding informative value — it is adding a line the eye must process. White space around the chart already differentiates it from the surrounding content. Removing the border reduces one more element the audience must look past to reach the data.

incorrect.message: Review the role of white space in visual design and consider what the border is actually adding to the chart.

steps.title: What you've learned: matching and simplifying charts

blocks.text: Chart choice is driven by the point you are making, not the data alone. Bar charts compare categories; line graphs show trends; pie charts express part-to-whole relationships. Once the right chart is chosen, remove every element that adds visual effort without adding information — border, gridlines, trailing zeros, rotated labels, unnecessary data labels. Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions are warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph.

remediation_steps.title: Scatterplots: exploratory vs. communicative — a closer look

blocks.text: A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. When you plot delivery distance against delivery time for yourself, you are exploring a relationship. That same chart can be designed to convey a finding to an audience — but it is not the default choice for a non-technical stakeholder presentation, because the audience must first understand what a scatterplot shows before they can read the point. If the relationship needs to go in front of the operations manager, consider whether a simpler chart can make the same point.

remediation_steps.title: Matching chart type to stakeholder point — a contrast

blocks.text: Bar charts compare values across categories — use one when the point is 'Lagos takes longer than Abuja.' Line graphs show how a value changes over time — use one when the point is 'Lagos delivery time has risen each week.' Pie charts express part-to-whole relationships — use one when the point is 'Lagos accounts for most of our total order volume' and the values sum to 100% (Lagos 57.1%, Abuja 28.6%, Kano 14.3%). Boxplots compare distributions but may be unfamiliar to non-technical audiences; a bar chart or line plot can often make the same point more directly.

Comparing pie slices looks easy, but it is not as easy as comparing bar lengths. A bar chart's common baseline makes differences immediately readable; two similar-sized pie slices are hard to rank correctly by eye. When precise comparison between categories matters, a bar chart is the stronger choice.

remediation_steps.title: Clutter elements and why they slow your audience down

blocks.text: Every element in a chart that does not add information adds cognitive effort. Gridlines can be deleted; if precise values matter, label the data point directly instead. A chart border is not adding informative value — white space separates parts of a visual better than a border. Data labels should be used sparingly, only where exact values are important; otherwise use the axis. Trailing zeroes on axis labels ('22.00') can be dropped ('22 min'). Diagonally rotated axis text is slower to read; abbreviate labels so they render horizontally.

Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be warranted, rather than working out how to read the graph. None of these changes alter the underlying delivery-time values — only how much visual effort it takes to read them.

remediation_steps.title: Border removal and white space — why it works

blocks.text: A chart border might seem to help by visually containing the chart on the slide. But the border is not adding informative value — it is adding a line the eye must process. White space around the chart already differentiates it from the surrounding content. Removing the border reduces one more element the audience must look past to reach the data. The same principle applies to gridlines: if the audience needs a precise value, label that data point directly rather than restoring the gridlines.
